w: Two Nazi shrines built in 1935 to house the sarcophagi of the 'blood witnesses' killed in the failed Beer Hall Putsch. The regime staged its cult of martyrs here until 9 January 1947, when the US Army tore down the temples' main architectural features - an act of denazification, leaving only bare platforms.
s: A Nazi martyrs' shrine the US Army tore down in 1947
_facts: Two structures erected by the Nazi Party in 1935
Housed sarcophagi of the sixteen 'Blutzeugen' (blood witnesses) killed in the 1923 Beer Hall Putsch
US Army destroyed the main architectural features on 9 January 1947 as denazification

w: One of Europe's biggest circuses, and one of only a handful in Western Europe with its own permanent building - a rarity shared with Paris's Cirque d'hiver, its Amiens cousin and Brussels's Cirque Royal. Munich's answer to a travelling big top: this one never has to strike the tent.
s: A circus that never has to strike the tent
_facts: One of the largest circuses in Europe
One of the few in Western Europe to occupy its own permanent building, alongside Cirque d'hiver de Paris, Cirque d'hiver d'Amiens and Cirque Royal in Brussels

w: A triumphal city gate anchoring the west side of Königsplatz. No fanfare, no ticket booth - just a stone threshold that most visitors to Munich's grand neoclassical square walk straight through without ever looking up.
s: The gate at Königsplatz nobody stops to read
_facts: A city gate built as a triumphal arch
Stands at the west side of Königsplatz

w: One of Munich's four royal avenues, laid out at the request of King Ludwig I as a boulevard 'worthy the kingdom' - and it still reads that way, its architectural uniformity unbroken since. State parades and funeral processions have marched its length; tourists mostly just stroll it.
s: The boulevard built to be worthy of a kingdom
_facts: One of Munich's four royal avenues, with Brienner Straße, Maximilianstraße and Prinzregentenstraße
Named after King Ludwig I of Bavaria, commissioned as a street 'worthy the kingdom'
Maintains architectural uniformity; has served for state parades and funeral processions

w: A Baroque hunting lodge built in 1715-17 for Elector Maximilian II Emanuel, made for stag-chasing rather than statecraft. It has since traded muskets for vestments: the archdiocese now runs it as a spiritual house and pastoral centre - a pleasure palace repurposed for quiet reflection.
s: A prince's hunting lodge, now a retreat for the archdiocese
_facts: Baroque maison de plaisance/hunting lodge built 1715-1717 for Elector Maximilian II Emanuel
Today serves as the archdiocese's spiritual house and pastoral centre

w: Twenty million zoological specimens, filed under Entomology, Invertebrates and Vertebrates - one of the largest natural history collections on Earth, and a working research institution rather than a visitor hall. Its first curator, Johann Baptist von Spix, set the tone for two centuries of cataloguing.
s: Twenty million specimens, one very serious filing system
_facts: Over 20 million zoological specimens
One of the largest natural history collections in the world
Sections: Entomology, Invertebrates, Vertebrates
First curator of zoology was Johann Baptist von Spix

w: A Benedictine monastery King Ludwig I built in 1835 to revive Bavaria's monastic life after secularisation stripped it bare - unusually, right in a city. Wrecked in WWII and only partly rebuilt, it still holds the tombs of Ludwig I and his queen, Therese, and once quietly acquired Andechs Abbey to fund itself.
s: A city-centre monastery holding a king's tomb
_facts: Founded 1835 by King Ludwig I to restore Bavaria's monastic life after secularisation
Byzantine-style church dedicated in 1850
Destroyed in WWII, only partly restored
Contains the tombs of King Ludwig I and Queen Therese of Saxe-Hildburghausen
Unusual for a Benedictine monastery to be located within a city
Ludwig gave it the former Andechs Abbey (secularised 1803) as a supporting priory
